codebook_metadata.title: EA_LT_4FMs_Codebook
codebook_metadata.purpose: Interpretive thematic analysis using 4 Fundamental Motivations of Existential Analysis and Logotherapy
sources: Längle, A. (1992). What Are We Looking for When We Search for Meaning? Ultimate Reality and Meaning, 15(4), 306-314.
Längle, A. (2002). Existential fundamental motivation. In Motivation, Consciousness and Self-Regulation (pp. 27-42). Nova Science Pub Inc.
Längle, A. (2003). The Art of Involving the Person – Fundamental Existential Motivations as the Structure of the Motivational Process. European Psychotherapy, 4(1), 25-36.

version_history.1.0: Initial codebook based on Längle (1992) - established 4FM structure
version_history.1.1: Added Längle (2002) - expanded with prerequisites, coping reactions, pathological outcomes
version_history.1.2: Added Längle (2003) - integrated motivational process structure, dialogical paradigm, assessment questions

inner_consent.description: The continuous activity of living with agreement to what one does, commits, or omits
inner_consent.source_quote: Seen more from the inside, i.e. seen more from a psychological point of view, we can describe the key for a fulfilling existence in finding a way of living with inner consent to what we do, to what we commit or omit.
inner_consent.citation: Längle, A. (2002). Existential fundamental motivation. In Motivation, Consciousness and Self-Regulation (pp. 27-42), p. 3.

dialogical_structure.description: Double dialogue - outer (with world/situation) and inner (with deepest feelings)
dialogical_structure.source_quote: In other words: to live with inner consent means that there is a continuous activity. It consists in a double dialogue: the one directed towards the outside with the question: What appeals me? What attracts or challenges me? Where am I needed, what do I want to do in this situation?... The other side of the dialogue runs inwardly. Whatever I decide to do – I cannot leave myself aside, if I want to experience my existence (and find meaning).
dialogical_structure.citation: Längle, A. (2002). Existential fundamental motivation. In Motivation, Consciousness and Self-Regulation (pp. 27-42), p. 3.

existential_analysis_definition.description: Phenomenological-personal psychotherapy enabling free experience, authentic decisions, and responsible dealing with self and world
existential_analysis_definition.source_quote: A scientifically definition of Existential Analysis describes it as a phenomenological-personal psychotherapy with the aim of enabling a person to experience his life freely at the spiritual and emotional levels, to arrive at authentic decisions and to come to a responsible way of dealing with himself and the world around.
existential_analysis_definition.citation: Längle, A. (2002). Existential fundamental motivation. In Motivation, Consciousness and Self-Regulation (pp. 27-42), p. 3.

motivation_existential_definition.description: Involvement of the person, initiating personal processes by provocation in some kind of vis-à-vis
motivation_existential_definition.source_quote: In other words, seen from an existential point of view, motivation means involvement of the person, initiating the personal processes by provocation in some kind of vis-à-vis.
motivation_existential_definition.citation: Längle, A. (2003). The Art of Involving the Person. European Psychotherapy, 4(1), p. 29.

being_in_the_world.description: The notion providing ground on which personal forces are activated through perceptive encounter
being_in_the_world.source_quote: Seen in that light, the notion of 'being-in-the-world' provides the ground, on which personal forces are activated. This happens by a perceptive encounter with some form of otherness or with oneself.
being_in_the_world.citation: Längle, A. (2003). The Art of Involving the Person. European Psychotherapy, 4(1), p. 30.

dialogical_being.description: Humans as essentially dialogical, prone to exchange with others; being in continuous communication
dialogical_being.source_quote: Being oneself as a person means being in communication – being in a continuous intrapersonal and interpersonal exchange of contents and values. It means fine-tuning the outer with the inner reality and vice versa, coordinating oneself with the objective meaning of the situation.
dialogical_being.citation: Längle, A. (2003). The Art of Involving the Person. European Psychotherapy, 4(1), p. 28.

provocation.description: Being called by something that confronts, challenges, engages us; starting point of motivation
provocation.source_quote: As dialogical beings we expect and look for something or someone who 'speaks' to us, calls us, needs us, talks to us, looks for us, challenges us. We get the necessary provocation through everything which confronts us, which challenges us, which engages us. At exactly that moment the object before us starts 'speaking' to us. Being provoked means being called. This provocation is the starting point for any motivation.
provocation.citation: Längle, A. (2003). The Art of Involving the Person. European Psychotherapy, 4(1), p. 29.

motivational_process.description: Three-step process of involving the person through recognition, harmonization, and inner consent

three_steps.name: Recognizing
three_steps.description: Recognizing something in its worth or value, in as far as it speaks to us
three_steps.source_quote: Recognizing something in its worth or value, in as far as it speaks to us. This is often a challenge demanding action on our part. What a situation 'pro-'vokes in us is indicative of or points to the situational meaning involved. To recognize this inner movement lays way to find personal meaning.
three_steps.citation: Längle, A. (2003). The Art of Involving the Person. European Psychotherapy, 4(1), p. 29.

three_steps.name: Harmonizing
three_steps.description: Bringing perceived value into accordance with inner reality
three_steps.source_quote: Harmonizing. Bringing the perceived value, challenge or meaning into accordance with our inner reality (i.e. examining the congruence with the rest of our values, with attitudes, abilities and capabilities and with our conscience etc.).
three_steps.citation: Längle, A. (2003). The Art of Involving the Person. European Psychotherapy, 4(1), p. 29.

three_steps.name: Giving inner consent
three_steps.description: Consenting to active involvement, leading to presence of inner person in actions
three_steps.source_quote: Giving inner consent to one's own active involvement. This consent and the act of harmonizing the new value with one's personal reality lead to the presence of the inner person in one's actions and to the integration of the new value and the person into a wider context (meaning).
three_steps.citation: Längle, A. (2003). The Art of Involving the Person. European Psychotherapy, 4(1), p. 29.

note_on_person_omission.description: Omitting the person results in reflex/reaction rather than true action
note_on_person_omission.source_quote: Omitting the person in the motivational process, according to our opinion, misses the main thrust of human motivation. Instead it focuses on a sort of reflex or reaction, but no 'action'. Any act or deed is defined as a decided act and is therefore voluntary and free.
note_on_person_omission.citation: Längle, A. (2003). The Art of Involving the Person. European Psychotherapy, 4(1), p. 29.

structure_of_will.description: Free and realistic will is based on four elements beyond meaning

elements.name: Real ability and capacity
elements.description: The actual ability and capacity of the subject
elements.source_quote: Free and realistic will is based on three more elements: 1. On the real ability and capacity of the subject;
elements.citation: Längle, A. (2003). The Art of Involving the Person. European Psychotherapy, 4(1), pp. 29-30.

elements.name: Emotional perception of value
elements.description: The emotional perception of the situational value
elements.source_quote: 2. On the emotional perception of the situational value;
elements.citation: Längle, A. (2003). The Art of Involving the Person. European Psychotherapy, 4(1), p. 30.

elements.name: Inner permission
elements.description: Inner permission for the act, emerging from agreement with concepts of life and morality
elements.source_quote: 3. On the inner permission for that act, emerging from an agreement with one's concepts of life and morality.
elements.citation: Längle, A. (2003). The Art of Involving the Person. European Psychotherapy, 4(1), p. 30.

elements.name: Meaning
elements.description: Meaning as the motor in free will (Frankl's contribution)
elements.source_quote: FRANKL (1970, 37-44; 1987, 101-104) saw meaning as the motor in free will.
elements.citation: Längle, A. (2003). The Art of Involving the Person. European Psychotherapy, 4(1), p. 29.

relationship_to_FMs.description: These four elements correspond to the four fundamental motivations
relationship_to_FMs.note: Element 1 (ability) relates to FM1 (Can I be?), Element 2 (value) relates to FM2 (Do I like?), Element 3 (permission) relates to FM3 (May I?), Element 4 (meaning) relates to FM4 (For what?)

interpersonal_paradigm.description: Modern EA's shift from individualistic paradigm to interpersonal paradigm

contrast_with_frankl.frankl_approach: Individualistic thinking, reducing motivation to concept of will
contrast_with_frankl.source_quote: However, in the motivational angle of his theory, Frankl may have adopted some individualistic thinking by tracing back and reducing the concept of existential motivation to the concept of will.
contrast_with_frankl.citation: Längle, A. (2003). The Art of Involving the Person. European Psychotherapy, 4(1), p. 27.

modern_approach.description: Interpersonal paradigm based on dialogical being, exchange with others
modern_approach.source_quote: As a complement and counterweight to the individualistic paradigm of freedom and personal will, which laid groundwork for the development of this postmodern era, we now propose an interpersonal paradigm.
modern_approach.citation: Längle, A. (2003). The Art of Involving the Person. European Psychotherapy, 4(1), p. 28.

need_for_the_other.description: No 'me' without 'you'; being oneself requires the field of tension of the 'between'
need_for_the_other.source_quote: Being oneself, finding oneself needs the field of tension of the 'inter-', the 'between', the 'aida' as the Japanese say (KIMURA 1982; 1995, 103ff.). This spiritual need for communication and dialogue is also underlined by the numerous personality disorders related to the loss of self! – There is no 'me' without a 'you', as both Buber and Frankl explaining.
need_for_the_other.citation: Längle, A. (2003). The Art of Involving the Person. European Psychotherapy, 4(1), p. 28.

alternative_names: The World – Dealing with Conditions and Possibilities
fundamental_motivations.description: The fundamental question of whether one can claim one's place in the world under given conditions and possibilities. Concerns protection, space, and support in existence.
fundamental_motivations.fundamental_question: I am - but can I be?
fundamental_motivations.practical_question: Can I claim my place in this world under the conditions and with the possibilities I have?
fundamental_motivations.source_quote_2003: But I am here, which sets before me the fundamental question of existence: I am – but can I be? To ask a more practical version of this question I need only apply it to my own situation. In that case, I may ask myself: Can I claim my place in this world under the conditions and with the possibilities I have?
fundamental_motivations.citation_2003: Längle, A. (2003). The Art of Involving the Person. European Psychotherapy, 4(1), p. 31.
fundamental_motivations.source_quote_2002: The first condition arises from the simple fact that I am here at all, that I am in the world... This puts the fundamental question of existence before me: I am - can I be? Can I claim my place in this world under the conditions and with the possibilities I have?
fundamental_motivations.citation_2002: Längle, A. (2002). Existential fundamental motivation. In Motivation, Consciousness and Self-Regulation (pp. 27-42), pp. 4-5.
fundamental_motivations.source_quote_1992: Meaning is therefore always orientation by the true, by what is and by what is experienced as reality. Meaning is unconditionally realistic. The person living meaningfully will face and grasp the facts.
fundamental_motivations.citation_1992: Längle, A. (1992). What Are We Looking for When We Search for Meaning? Ultimate Reality and Meaning, 15(4), p. 312.
fundamental_motivations.related_will_element: Real ability and capacity of the subject

prerequisites.name: Protection
prerequisites.description: Experiencing acceptance and feeling at home
prerequisites.source_quote: This demands three things: protection, space and support. - Do I enjoy protection, acceptance, do I feel at home somewhere?
prerequisites.citation: Längle, A. (2002). Existential fundamental motivation. In Motivation, Consciousness and Self-Regulation (pp. 27-42), p. 5.
prerequisites.assessment_question: Do I enjoy protection, acceptance, do I feel at home somewhere?
prerequisites.citation_assessment: Längle, A. (2003). The Art of Involving the Person. European Psychotherapy, 4(1), p. 31.

prerequisites.name: Space
prerequisites.description: Having enough space for being there
prerequisites.source_quote: - Do I have enough space for being there?
prerequisites.citation: Längle, A. (2002). Existential fundamental motivation. In Motivation, Consciousness and Self-Regulation (pp. 27-42), p. 5.
prerequisites.assessment_question: Do I have enough space to be here?
prerequisites.citation_assessment: Längle, A. (2003). The Art of Involving the Person. European Psychotherapy, 4(1), p. 31.

prerequisites.name: Support
prerequisites.source_quote: - Where do I find support in my life?
prerequisites.citation: Längle, A. (2002). Existential fundamental motivation. In Motivation, Consciousness and Self-Regulation (pp. 27-42), p. 5.
prerequisites.assessment_question: Where do I find support in my life?
prerequisites.citation_assessment: Längle, A. (2003). The Art of Involving the Person. European Psychotherapy, 4(1), p. 31.

positive_outcomes_if_fulfilled.source_quote: if I do have these three things, I will be able to feel trust in the world and confidence in myself, maybe even faith in God. The sum of these experiences of trust is the fundamental trust, the trust in whatever I feel as being the last support in my life.
positive_outcomes_if_fulfilled.citation: Längle, A. (2002). Existential fundamental motivation. In Motivation, Consciousness and Self-Regulation (pp. 27-42), p. 5.

positive_outcomes_if_fulfilled.source_quote: I will be able to feel trust in the world and confidence in myself
positive_outcomes_if_fulfilled.citation: Längle, A. (2002). Existential fundamental motivation. In Motivation, Consciousness and Self-Regulation (pp. 27-42), p. 5.

positive_outcomes_if_fulfilled.source_quote: The sum of these experiences of trust is the fundamental trust, the trust in whatever I consider to be the last and final support in my life.
positive_outcomes_if_fulfilled.citation: Längle, A. (2003). The Art of Involving the Person. European Psychotherapy, 4(1), p. 31.
Längle, A. (2003). The Art of Involving the Person. European Psychotherapy, 4(1), p. 31.

negative_outcomes_if_not_fulfilled.source_quote: If these conditions of existence are not met, the result will be restlessness, insecurity and fear
negative_outcomes_if_not_fulfilled.citation: Längle, A. (2003). The Art of Involving the Person. European Psychotherapy, 4(1), p. 31.

negative_outcomes_if_not_fulfilled.source_quote: If these conditions of existence are not met, the result will be restlessness, insecurity and fear
negative_outcomes_if_not_fulfilled.citation: Längle, A. (2003). The Art of Involving the Person. European Psychotherapy, 4(1), p. 31.

negative_outcomes_if_not_fulfilled.source_quote: If these conditions of existence are not met, the result will be restlessness, insecurity and fear
negative_outcomes_if_not_fulfilled.citation: Längle, A. (2003). The Art of Involving the Person. European Psychotherapy, 4(1), p. 31.

accept.description: Readiness to occupy space, rely on support, trust protection, and 'be there'
accept.source_quote: To accept means to be ready to occupy the space, to rely on the support and to trust the protection; in short 'to be there' and not to flee.
accept.citation: Längle, A. (2003). The Art of Involving the Person. European Psychotherapy, 4(1), p. 32.

endure.description: Strength to persist despite difficulty; supporting what cannot be changed
endure.source_quote: To endure means to have the strength to persist in spite of whatever is difficult, menacing or unalterable, and to 'support' what cannot be changed.
endure.citation: Längle, A. (2003). The Art of Involving the Person. European Psychotherapy, 4(1), p. 32.

accept_and_let_be.description: Accepting given conditions while maintaining one's own space
accept_and_let_be.source_quote: Therefore, to accept means to let each other be, because there is still enough space for me, and the circumstances do not threaten me anymore.
accept_and_let_be.citation: Längle, A. (2003). The Art of Involving the Person. European Psychotherapy, 4(1), p. 32.

subject_concept.description: Being subject to or dependent upon conditions; yet conditions are reliable and steady
subject_concept.source_quote: Life imposes certain conditions on me, and the world has its laws, which I can only accept. This idea is expressed in the word 'subject' in the sense of 'being subject to or dependent upon'. On the other hand, these conditions are reliable, solid and steady.
subject_concept.citation: Längle, A. (2003). The Art of Involving the Person. European Psychotherapy, 4(1), p. 32.

coping_reactions.source_quote: Each fundamental motivation has four types of coping reactions: the basic reaction type – here this would be avoidance or flight
coping_reactions.citation: Längle, A. (2002). Existential fundamental motivation. In Motivation, Consciousness and Self-Regulation (pp. 27-42), p. 5.

coping_reactions.reaction: Overactivity like fighting bacteria by compulsive washing
coping_reactions.source_quote: the paradoxical reaction type or activism – here this would be overactivity like fighting bacteria by compulsive washing
coping_reactions.citation: Längle, A. (2002). Existential fundamental motivation. In Motivation, Consciousness and Self-Regulation (pp. 27-42), p. 5.

coping_reactions.source_quote: the third type of coping reaction is a specific aggression (Längle 1998b) – here it would be a destructive aggression such as hate
coping_reactions.citation: Längle, A. (2002). Existential fundamental motivation. In Motivation, Consciousness and Self-Regulation (pp. 27-42), p. 5.

coping_reactions.reaction: Denial or pretending to be non-existent
coping_reactions.source_quote: the last type of coping reaction is a reflex of freezing, of death imitation with paralysis – here denial or pretending to be non-existent.
coping_reactions.citation: Längle, A. (2002). Existential fundamental motivation. In Motivation, Consciousness and Self-Regulation (pp. 27-42), p. 5.

psychodynamic_note.description: When ability to accept and endure fails, psychodynamics take over as coping reactions
psychodynamic_note.source_quote: Human beings procure the space they need with their ability to tolerate and to accept conditions. If this is not the case, psychodynamic forces take over the guidance in the form of coping reactions, which aim secure life
psychodynamic_note.citation: Längle, A. (2003). The Art of Involving the Person. European Psychotherapy, 4(1), p. 32.

sub_themes.description: The fundamental ontological experience of existence within a network of effects
sub_themes.source_quote: Man sees that the world is continually effecting him. Acting, he realises that he in turn has an effect on the world. In this way he experiences his special relation with the world, in which he stands. This 'being-in-the-world' (Heidegger) is the fundamental state man finds himself in, his basic ontological experience.
sub_themes.citation: Längle, A. (1992). What Are We Looking for When We Search for Meaning? Ultimate Reality and Meaning, 15(4), pp. 309-310.
indicators: Coming into being and passing away

sub_themes.description: Question about the ground of existence and interrelatedness of things
sub_themes.source_quote: The question of meaning on the ontological level is a question to the ground out of which things are and out of which man himself is (Grundfrage)! When man asks about the ground for things and for his own being, he is asking the ontological question of meaning.
sub_themes.citation: Längle, A. (1992). What Are We Looking for When We Search for Meaning? Ultimate Reality and Meaning, 15(4), p. 310.
indicators: Anticipation that all things must be interrelated

sub_themes.description: The appropriate attitude toward the incomprehensible fact of existence
sub_themes.source_quote: The most adequate and traditional attitude towards the incomprehensible is one of astonishment. Basically, I can only be astonished that I am here at all.
sub_themes.citation: Längle, A. (2003). The Art of Involving the Person. European Psychotherapy, 4(1), p. 31.
indicators: Wonder at being here at all
Existence as island in ocean of ignorance

existential_needs.description: Need for factual reality to hold and support in order to act and receive effects
existential_needs.source_quote: He needs their ground to hold and support him, in order to act and receive effects.
existential_needs.citation: Längle, A. (1992). What Are We Looking for When We Search for Meaning? Ultimate Reality and Meaning, 15(4), p. 312.
manifestations: Wanting to be perceived by others
Wanting to be seen as what one is with specific faculties

alternative_names: Life – Dealing with Relationships and Emotions
fundamental_motivations.description: The fundamental question of whether it is good to be alive. Concerns the pathic dimension of existence - experiencing and suffering/enjoying life through relationships, time, and closeness.
fundamental_motivations.fundamental_question: I am alive – but do I like this fact? Is it good to be here?
fundamental_motivations.source_quote_2003: Therefore I am confronted with the fundamental question of life: I am alive – but do I like this fact? Is it good to be here? It is not only strain and suffering that can take away the joy of life. It may also be the superficiality of daily life and the self neglect of one's lifestyle that make life stale.
fundamental_motivations.citation_2003: Längle, A. (2003). The Art of Involving the Person. European Psychotherapy, 4(1), p. 32.
fundamental_motivations.source_quote_2002: Therefore I am confronted with the fundamental question of life: I am alive – do I like this fact? Is it good to be there? It is not only strain and suffering that can take away the joy of life. It may as well be the shallowness of daily life and the negligence in one's life style that make life stale.
fundamental_motivations.citation_2002: Längle, A. (2002). Existential fundamental motivation. In Motivation, Consciousness and Self-Regulation (pp. 27-42), p. 6.
fundamental_motivations.source_quote_1992: search for meaning includes the desire for the attractive, the desire for dealing with the valuable which man wants to give as much as to receive.
fundamental_motivations.citation_1992: Längle, A. (1992). What Are We Looking for When We Search for Meaning? Ultimate Reality and Meaning, 15(4), p. 312.
fundamental_motivations.related_will_element: Emotional perception of the situational value

pathic_dimension.description: Existence that does not simply happen but is experienced, suffered, or enjoyed
pathic_dimension.source_quote: Simply being there is not enough. We want our existence to be good, since it is more than a mere fact. It has a 'pathic dimension', which means that it does not simply happen, but that we experience and suffer or enjoy it. Being alive means to cry and to laugh, to experience joy and suffering, to go through pleasant and unpleasant things, to be lucky or unlucky and to experience worth and worthlessness.
pathic_dimension.citation: Längle, A. (2003). The Art of Involving the Person. European Psychotherapy, 4(1), p. 32.

prerequisites.name: Relationship
prerequisites.description: Having relationships where closeness and community are experienced
prerequisites.source_quote: In order to seize life, to love it, I need three things: relationship, time and closeness.
prerequisites.citation: Längle, A. (2003). The Art of Involving the Person. European Psychotherapy, 4(1), p. 32.
prerequisites.assessment_question: Do I have relationships, in which I experience closeness, in which I invest time and which give me a sense of community?
prerequisites.citation_assessment: Längle, A. (2003). The Art of Involving the Person. European Psychotherapy, 4(1), p. 32.

prerequisites.name: Time
prerequisites.description: Taking time for valuable things, giving away part of one's life
prerequisites.source_quote: To take time for something means to give away a part of one's life while spending it with someone or something.
prerequisites.citation: Längle, A. (2003). The Art of Involving the Person. European Psychotherapy, 4(1), p. 32.
prerequisites.assessment_question: What do I take time for? Do I take time for valuable things, which are worth my time?
prerequisites.citation_assessment: Längle, A. (2003). The Art of Involving the Person. European Psychotherapy, 4(1), p. 32.

prerequisites.name: Closeness
prerequisites.description: Ability to feel and maintain closeness to things, animals, and people
prerequisites.source_quote: - Can I feel close and maintain closeness to things, plants, animals and people? Can I admit the closeness of someone else?
prerequisites.citation: Längle, A. (2002). Existential fundamental motivation. In Motivation, Consciousness and Self-Regulation (pp. 27-42), p. 6.
prerequisites.assessment_question: Do I feel close and maintain closeness to things, plants, animals and people? Do I permit myself to come close to another person?
prerequisites.citation_assessment: Längle, A. (2003). The Art of Involving the Person. European Psychotherapy, 4(1), p. 32.

positive_outcomes_if_fulfilled.source_quote: if these three conditions are fulfilled, I can experience myself as being in harmony with the world and with myself, and I can sense the depth of life.
positive_outcomes_if_fulfilled.citation: Längle, A. (2003). The Art of Involving the Person. European Psychotherapy, 4(1), p. 32.

positive_outcomes_if_fulfilled.source_quote: I can sense the depth of life.
positive_outcomes_if_fulfilled.citation: Längle, A. (2003). The Art of Involving the Person. European Psychotherapy, 4(1), p. 32.

positive_outcomes_if_fulfilled.source_quote: These experiences form the fundamental value, the most profound feeling for the inherent value of life. Our experience of any and all values are shaped by this fundamental value, it colors the emotions and affects and represents our yardstick for anything we might feel to be of worth.
positive_outcomes_if_fulfilled.citation: Längle, A. (2003). The Art of Involving the Person. European Psychotherapy, 4(1), pp. 32-33.

negative_outcomes_if_not_fulfilled.source_quote: If relationships, closeness and time are lacking, longing will arise, then coldness and finally depression.
negative_outcomes_if_not_fulfilled.citation: Längle, A. (2003). The Art of Involving the Person. European Psychotherapy, 4(1), p. 32.

negative_outcomes_if_not_fulfilled.source_quote: If relationships, closeness and time are lacking, longing will arise, then coldness and finally depression.
negative_outcomes_if_not_fulfilled.citation: Längle, A. (2003). The Art of Involving the Person. European Psychotherapy, 4(1), p. 32.

negative_outcomes_if_not_fulfilled.source_quote: If relationships, closeness and time are lacking, longing will arise, then coldness and finally depression.
negative_outcomes_if_not_fulfilled.citation: Längle, A. (2003). The Art of Involving the Person. European Psychotherapy, 4(1), p. 32.

seize_life_carpe_diem.description: Turning toward people, things, animals, work, or self; moving toward, getting close
seize_life_carpe_diem.source_quote: I seize life (carpe diem), engage in it, when I turn toward other people, toward things, animals, intellectual work or to myself, when I move towards it, get close, get in touch or pull it towards me.
seize_life_carpe_diem.citation: Längle, A. (2003). The Art of Involving the Person. European Psychotherapy, 4(1), p. 33.

consent_to_being_touched.description: Allowing life to make one move freely; consenting to feelings
consent_to_being_touched.source_quote: This 'turning to' will make life reverberate within me. If life is to make me move freely, my consent to being touched (to my feelings) is a prerequisite.
consent_to_being_touched.citation: Längle, A. (2003). The Art of Involving the Person. European Psychotherapy, 4(1), p. 33.

grief_when_turning_to_loss.description: Turning toward loss results in grief
grief_when_turning_to_loss.source_quote: If I turn toward a loss, grief arises.
grief_when_turning_to_loss.citation: Längle, A. (2003). The Art of Involving the Person. European Psychotherapy, 4(1), p. 33.

coping_reactions.source_quote: The basic coping reaction on this level is regression.
coping_reactions.citation: Längle, A. (2002). Existential fundamental motivation. In Motivation, Consciousness and Self-Regulation (pp. 27-42), p. 6.

coping_reactions.reaction: Overprotection or achievement, typical forms of combating evil
coping_reactions.source_quote: The activism here is overprotection or achievement, typical forms of combating evil
coping_reactions.citation: Längle, A. (2002). Existential fundamental motivation. In Motivation, Consciousness and Self-Regulation (pp. 27-42), p. 6.

coping_reactions.reaction: Fury, rage to agitate and improve relationship
coping_reactions.source_quote: the typical aggression is fury, rage which does not lead to destruction, but wants to agitate the other person with the impulse to obtain or to improve the relationship.
coping_reactions.citation: Längle, A. (2002). Existential fundamental motivation. In Motivation, Consciousness and Self-Regulation (pp. 27-42), p. 6.

coping_reactions.source_quote: Resignation reaction of feigned death paralyzed half-way.
coping_reactions.citation: Längle, A. (2002). Existential fundamental motivation. In Motivation, Consciousness and Self-Regulation (pp. 27-42), p. 6.

sub_themes.description: Recognition that it matters what becomes of things and which effects result
sub_themes.source_quote: Man continually faces the axiological question of meaning: 'What is good about it?', 'What is it good for?' This expresses what Frankl (1982a, p. 221) calls the 'will to meaning'.
sub_themes.citation: Längle, A. (1992). What Are We Looking for When We Search for Meaning? Ultimate Reality and Meaning, 15(4), pp. 310-311.
indicators: Things connected with value of being

sub_themes.description: The fundamental experience that it is good to be
sub_themes.source_quote: He not only knows that he is, but that in itself it is also good to be (Längle, 1984, pp. 52ff.). With this finality things of the world rise out of the grey dawn of mere presence and receive the colour of value.
sub_themes.citation: Längle, A. (1992). What Are We Looking for When We Search for Meaning? Ultimate Reality and Meaning, 15(4), p. 310.
indicators: Things are more or less good

sub_themes.description: Equal capacity for happiness and suffering
sub_themes.source_quote: We experience happiness to the same extent and depth that we experience suffering. The amplitude of emotionality is equal in both directions, whether this suits us or not.
sub_themes.citation: Längle, A. (2003). The Art of Involving the Person. European Psychotherapy, 4(1), p. 32.

existential_needs.description: Need to engage with that which holds value, both giving and receiving
existential_needs.source_quote: the desire for dealing with the valuable which man wants to give as much as to receive.
existential_needs.citation: Längle, A. (1992). What Are We Looking for When We Search for Meaning? Ultimate Reality and Meaning, 15(4), p. 312.

fundamental_motivations.fm_name: MAY I BE LIKE THIS? (Being Oneself/Person)
alternative_names: Being a Person – Dealing with Uniqueness and Conscience
fundamental_motivations.description: The fundamental question of whether one has the right to be what one is and behave as one does. Concerns identity, self-knowledge, ethics, and authenticity through attention, justice, and appreciation.
fundamental_motivations.fundamental_question: I am myself – may I be like this? Do I feel free to be like that? Do I have the right to be what I am and to behave as I do?
fundamental_motivations.source_quote_2003: This places before me the fundamental question of being a person: I am myself – may I be like this? Do I feel free to be like that? Do I have the right to be what I am and to behave as I do? This is the domain of identity, of knowing oneself and of ethics.
fundamental_motivations.citation_2003: Längle, A. (2003). The Art of Involving the Person. European Psychotherapy, 4(1), p. 33.
fundamental_motivations.source_quote_2002: This puts before me the fundamental question of being a person: I am myself – may I be like this? Do I feel free to be like that? Do I have the right to be what I am and to behave as I do? – This is the plane of identity, of knowing oneself and of ethics.
fundamental_motivations.citation_2002: Längle, A. (2002). Existential fundamental motivation. In Motivation, Consciousness and Self-Regulation (pp. 27-42), p. 7.
fundamental_motivations.source_quote_1992: the need for relations is alive in meaning, for relating to oneself (responsibility) as well as to others, which enables the justification of existence.
fundamental_motivations.citation_1992: Längle, A. (1992). What Are We Looking for When We Search for Meaning? Ultimate Reality and Meaning, 15(4), p. 312.
fundamental_motivations.related_will_element: Inner permission for the act, emerging from agreement with concepts of life and morality

singularity_and_separateness.description: Awareness of being separate, different, on one's own in existence
singularity_and_separateness.source_quote: In spite of my being related to life and to people, I am aware of my being separate, different. There is a singularity that makes me an 'I' and distinguishes me from everybody else. I realize that I am on my own, that I have to master my existence myself and that, basically, I am alone and maybe even lonely.
singularity_and_separateness.citation: Längle, A. (2003). The Art of Involving the Person. European Psychotherapy, 4(1), p. 33.

diversity_and_respect.description: Recognition of uniqueness and beauty in all singular things, evoking respect
diversity_and_respect.source_quote: But in addition to my solitude, there is so much more that is equally singular. The diversity, beauty and uniqueness in all of this make me feel respect for it.
diversity_and_respect.citation: Längle, A. (2003). The Art of Involving the Person. European Psychotherapy, 4(1), p. 33.

prerequisites.name: Attention
prerequisites.description: Being seen, having one's uniqueness considered and boundaries respected
prerequisites.source_quote: In order to succeed, it is necessary to have experienced three things: Attention, justice and appreciation.
prerequisites.citation: Längle, A. (2003). The Art of Involving the Person. European Psychotherapy, 4(1), p. 33.
prerequisites.assessment_question: Who sees me? Who considers my uniqueness and respects my boundaries?
prerequisites.citation_assessment: Längle, A. (2003). The Art of Involving the Person. European Psychotherapy, 4(1), p. 33.

prerequisites.name: Justice
prerequisites.citation: Längle, A. (2002). Existential fundamental motivation. In Motivation, Consciousness and Self-Regulation (pp. 27-42), p. 7.
prerequisites.citation_assessment: Längle, A. (2003). The Art of Involving the Person. European Psychotherapy, 4(1), p. 33.

prerequisites.name: Appreciation
prerequisites.description: Being appreciated and able to appreciate oneself
prerequisites.source_quote: - For what am I appreciated – for what can I appreciate myself?
prerequisites.citation: Längle, A. (2002). Existential fundamental motivation. In Motivation, Consciousness and Self-Regulation (pp. 27-42), p. 7.
prerequisites.assessment_question: For what am I appreciated – for what can I appreciate myself?
prerequisites.citation_assessment: Längle, A. (2003). The Art of Involving the Person. European Psychotherapy, 4(1), p. 33.

positive_outcomes_if_fulfilled.source_quote: If, on the other hand, I experience these qualities, I will find myself, find my authenticity, my relief and my self-respect.
positive_outcomes_if_fulfilled.citation: Längle, A. (2003). The Art of Involving the Person. European Psychotherapy, 4(1), p. 33.

positive_outcomes_if_fulfilled.source_quote: I will find myself, find my authenticity, my relief and my self-respect.
positive_outcomes_if_fulfilled.citation: Längle, A. (2003). The Art of Involving the Person. European Psychotherapy, 4(1), p. 33.

positive_outcomes_if_fulfilled.source_quote: I will find myself, find my authenticity, my relief and my self-respect.
positive_outcomes_if_fulfilled.citation: Längle, A. (2003). The Art of Involving the Person. European Psychotherapy, 4(1), p. 33.

positive_outcomes_if_fulfilled.source_quote: I will find myself, find my authenticity, my relief and my self-respect.
positive_outcomes_if_fulfilled.citation: Längle, A. (2003). The Art of Involving the Person. European Psychotherapy, 4(1), p. 33.

positive_outcomes_if_fulfilled.source_quote: The sum of these experiences builds one's worth, the most profound worth of what identifies my own self at its core: My self-esteem.
positive_outcomes_if_fulfilled.citation: Längle, A. (2003). The Art of Involving the Person. European Psychotherapy, 4(1), p. 33.

negative_outcomes_if_not_fulfilled.source_quote: If these experiences are missing, loneliness will be the result, hysteria (histrionic disorders) as well as a need to hide behind shame.
negative_outcomes_if_not_fulfilled.citation: Längle, A. (2003). The Art of Involving the Person. European Psychotherapy, 4(1), p. 33.

negative_outcomes_if_not_fulfilled.source_quote: If these experiences are missing, loneliness will be the result, hysteria (histrionic disorders) as well as a need to hide behind shame.
negative_outcomes_if_not_fulfilled.citation: Längle, A. (2003). The Art of Involving the Person. European Psychotherapy, 4(1), p. 33.

negative_outcomes_if_not_fulfilled.source_quote: If these experiences are missing, loneliness will be the result, hysteria (histrionic disorders) as well as a need to hide behind shame.
negative_outcomes_if_not_fulfilled.citation: Längle, A. (2003). The Art of Involving the Person. European Psychotherapy, 4(1), p. 33.

say_yes_to_myself.description: Looking at others, encountering them, while delimiting self and standing by one's own
say_yes_to_myself.source_quote: I also have to say 'yes to myself'. This requires my active participation: To look at other people, to encounter them and, at the same time, to delineate myself and to stand by my own, and to refuse whatever does not correspond to myself.
say_yes_to_myself.citation: Längle, A. (2003). The Art of Involving the Person. European Psychotherapy, 4(1), p. 33.

encounter.description: Bridge to the other, finding essence in the 'you' and participating in self-appreciation
encounter.source_quote: Encounter represents the necessary bridge to the other, causes me find his or her essence as well as my own 'I in the you'. Thus, I participate in my self-appreciation, attain my self-acceptance.
encounter.citation: Längle, A. (2003). The Art of Involving the Person. European Psychotherapy, 4(1), p. 33.

regret.description: Refusing what does not correspond to oneself
regret.source_quote: and to refuse whatever does not correspond to myself. Encounter and regret are the two means by which we can live our authenticity without ending up in solitude.
regret.citation: Längle, A. (2003). The Art of Involving the Person. European Psychotherapy, 4(1), p. 33.

coping_reactions.source_quote: The coping reactions of this motivation are: distancing oneself as the basic reaction
coping_reactions.citation: Längle, A. (2002). Existential fundamental motivation. In Motivation, Consciousness and Self-Regulation (pp. 27-42), p. 7.

coping_reactions.reaction: Stubborn insistence and leading a functional life
coping_reactions.source_quote: stubborn insistence and leading a functional life as form of activism.
coping_reactions.citation: Längle, A. (2002). Existential fundamental motivation. In Motivation, Consciousness and Self-Regulation (pp. 27-42), p. 7.

coping_reactions.source_quote: The typical aggressive reaction consists in indignation, annoyance – anger, reproach.
coping_reactions.citation: Längle, A. (2002). Existential fundamental motivation. In Motivation, Consciousness and Self-Regulation (pp. 27-42), p. 7.

coping_reactions.reaction: Dissociation of bodily integrity, dividing and splitting of emotion and cognition
coping_reactions.source_quote: The freezing type of reaction at this level are dissociation of the bodily integrity, dividing and splitting of emotion and cognition.
coping_reactions.citation: Längle, A. (2002). Existential fundamental motivation. In Motivation, Consciousness and Self-Regulation (pp. 27-42), p. 7.

sub_themes.description: The challenge to meaningful action and personal contribution
sub_themes.source_quote: This is the existential question of meaning. He finds himself up against the question: 'What do I do as a free, creative and responsible person in the middle of this world?' This is how man knows himself as fundamentally questioned in his existence (Längle, 1988, pp. 10ff.), challenged towards his contribution to the formation of this life and this world in the knowledge of an indispensable relation, personal responsibility and justification.
sub_themes.citation: Längle, A. (1992). What Are We Looking for When We Search for Meaning? Ultimate Reality and Meaning, 15(4), p. 311.
indicators: Personal contribution to life and world

sub_themes.description: Experience of consequences and accountability for one's actions
sub_themes.source_quote: His will to justification arises out of the necessity to be at home and accepted in the social structure, as well as in the structure of biographical life, where everything he has done, finally has to do with himself. This is what man experiences as responsibility.
sub_themes.citation: Längle, A. (1992). What Are We Looking for When We Search for Meaning? Ultimate Reality and Meaning, 15(4), p. 311.
indicators: Present and future effects of what has been done

sub_themes.description: The right to live amidst all of life's relations, especially social structure
sub_themes.source_quote: His will to justification arises out of the necessity to be at home and accepted in the social structure, as well as in the structure of biographical life
sub_themes.citation: Längle, A. (1992). What Are We Looking for When We Search for Meaning? Ultimate Reality and Meaning, 15(4), p. 311.
indicators: Being at home in social structure

existential_needs.description: Need to preserve faithfulness to oneself in decision-making
existential_needs.source_quote: Throughout this process he is ever looking for possibilities to make decisions in such a way that his personal integrity (in the sense of responsibility and faithfulness to oneself) is preserved.
existential_needs.citation: Längle, A. (1992). What Are We Looking for When We Search for Meaning? Ultimate Reality and Meaning, 15(4), p. 313.
manifestations: Entering personal relation by making decisions

alternative_names: Meaning – Dealing with Becoming, Future and Commitment
fundamental_motivations.description: The fundamental question of what one's life is about. Recognition of meaning through field of activity, structural context, and value to be realized. Concerns transcending oneself to find fulfillment and be fruitful.
fundamental_motivations.fundamental_question: I am here – but for what purpose?
fundamental_motivations.source_quote_2003: The transience of life confronts us with the question of meaning of our existence: I am here – but for what purpose?
fundamental_motivations.citation_2003: Längle, A. (2003). The Art of Involving the Person. European Psychotherapy, 4(1), p. 34.
fundamental_motivations.source_quote_2002: Thus the transience of life puts before us the question of meaning of our existence: I am there – for what is it good?
fundamental_motivations.citation_2002: Längle, A. (2002). Existential fundamental motivation. In Motivation, Consciousness and Self-Regulation (pp. 27-42), p. 8.
fundamental_motivations.source_quote_1992: man finally becomes ready to act, after he has ultimately arrived at the 'will to meaning' by the steps of the three noetic motivations. Knowing at this point what he can do, what he wants to do and what he may do, he finally realises what he should do - ready to engage himself thanks to his will to act.
fundamental_motivations.citation_1992: Längle, A. (1992). What Are We Looking for When We Search for Meaning? Ultimate Reality and Meaning, 15(4), pp. 311-312.
fundamental_motivations.motivation: Will to act / Will to meaning
fundamental_motivations.related_will_element: Meaning as the motor in free will

transcendence_necessity.description: Need to transcend oneself for fulfillment and fruitfulness; avoiding loneliness and triviality
transcendence_necessity.source_quote: It does not suffice to simply be there and to have found oneself. In a sense, we have to transcend ourselves, if we want to find fulfillment in life and to be fertile. Without this self-transcendence, moving beyond ourselves toward something greater, we are condemned to a life of loneliness and triviality.
transcendence_necessity.citation: Längle, A. (2003). The Art of Involving the Person. European Psychotherapy, 4(1), p. 34.

prerequisites.name: Field of activity
prerequisites.description: A place where one feels needed and can be productive
prerequisites.source_quote: To experience this sense of direction in life, three things are necessary: A field of activity, a structural context and a value to be realized in the future.
prerequisites.citation: Längle, A. (2003). The Art of Involving the Person. European Psychotherapy, 4(1), p. 34.
prerequisites.assessment_question: Is there a place where I feel needed, where I can be productive?
prerequisites.citation_assessment: Längle, A. (2003). The Art of Involving the Person. European Psychotherapy, 4(1), p. 34.

prerequisites.name: Structural context
prerequisites.description: Larger context providing structure and orientation; where one wants to be integrated
prerequisites.source_quote: – Do I see and experience myself in a larger context that provides structure and orientation to my life? Where I want to be integrated?
prerequisites.citation: Längle, A. (2003). The Art of Involving the Person. European Psychotherapy, 4(1), p. 34.
prerequisites.assessment_question: Do I see and experience myself in a larger context that provides structure and orientation to my life? Where I want to be integrated?
prerequisites.citation_assessment: Längle, A. (2003). The Art of Involving the Person. European Psychotherapy, 4(1), p. 34.

prerequisites.name: Value to be realized in the future
prerequisites.description: Something that should still be realized in one's life
prerequisites.source_quote: – Is there anything that should still be realized or accomplished in my life?
prerequisites.citation: Längle, A. (2003). The Art of Involving the Person. European Psychotherapy, 4(1), p. 34.
prerequisites.assessment_question: Is there anything that should still be realized or accomplished in my life?
prerequisites.citation_assessment: Längle, A. (2003). The Art of Involving the Person. European Psychotherapy, 4(1), p. 34.

positive_outcomes_if_fulfilled.source_quote: If, on the contrary, these conditions are met, I will be capable of dedication and action and, finally, of my own form of religious belief.
positive_outcomes_if_fulfilled.citation: Längle, A. (2003). The Art of Involving the Person. European Psychotherapy, 4(1), p. 34.

positive_outcomes_if_fulfilled.source_quote: I will be capable of dedication and action and, finally, of my own form of religious belief.
positive_outcomes_if_fulfilled.citation: Längle, A. (2003). The Art of Involving the Person. European Psychotherapy, 4(1), p. 34.

positive_outcomes_if_fulfilled.outcome: Meaning of life and sense of fulfillment
positive_outcomes_if_fulfilled.source_quote: The sum of these experiences adds up to the meaning of life and leads to a sense of fulfillment.
positive_outcomes_if_fulfilled.citation: Längle, A. (2003). The Art of Involving the Person. European Psychotherapy, 4(1), p. 34.

negative_outcomes_if_not_fulfilled.source_quote: If I cannot answer these questions in the affirmative, the result will be a feeling of emptiness, frustration, even despair and may frequently result in addiction or suicidal tendencies.
negative_outcomes_if_not_fulfilled.citation: Längle, A. (2003). The Art of Involving the Person. European Psychotherapy, 4(1), p. 34.

negative_outcomes_if_not_fulfilled.source_quote: If I cannot answer these questions in the affirmative, the result will be a feeling of emptiness, frustration, even despair and may frequently result in addiction or suicidal tendencies.
negative_outcomes_if_not_fulfilled.citation: Längle, A. (2003). The Art of Involving the Person. European Psychotherapy, 4(1), p. 34.

negative_outcomes_if_not_fulfilled.source_quote: If I cannot answer these questions in the affirmative, the result will be a feeling of emptiness, frustration, even despair and may frequently result in addiction or suicidal tendencies.
negative_outcomes_if_not_fulfilled.citation: Längle, A. (2003). The Art of Involving the Person. European Psychotherapy, 4(1), p. 34.

negative_outcomes_if_not_fulfilled.source_quote: may frequently result in addiction or suicidal tendencies.
negative_outcomes_if_not_fulfilled.citation: Längle, A. (2003). The Art of Involving the Person. European Psychotherapy, 4(1), p. 34.

negative_outcomes_if_not_fulfilled.source_quote: may frequently result in addiction or suicidal tendencies.
negative_outcomes_if_not_fulfilled.citation: Längle, A. (2003). The Art of Involving the Person. European Psychotherapy, 4(1), p. 34.

phenomenological_attitude_of_openness.description: Dealing with questions put before one in each situation; responding to challenges
phenomenological_attitude_of_openness.source_quote: Instead, a phenomenological attitude is needed to which we referred at the beginning. This attitude of openness represents the existential access to meaning in life: the ability to deal with the questions put before me in each situation (FRANKL 1973, XV, 62). How am I challenged by this moment, and how should I respond?
phenomenological_attitude_of_openness.citation: Längle, A. (2003). The Art of Involving the Person. European Psychotherapy, 4(1), p. 34.

bring_into_agreement.description: Examining whether what one is doing is good for others, self, future, environment
bring_into_agreement.source_quote: My active part in this attitude of openness is to bring myself into agreement with the situation, to examine whether what I am doing is really a good thing for others, for myself, for the future, for my environment. If I act accordingly, my existence will be fulfilling.
bring_into_agreement.citation: Längle, A. (2003). The Art of Involving the Person. European Psychotherapy, 4(1), p. 34.

dialogical_structure_with_life.description: Not only what I expect from life, but what life wants from me
dialogical_structure_with_life.source_quote: The meaningful thing is not only what I can expect from life, but, in accordance with the dialogical structure of existence, it is equally important what life wants from me. And what the moment expects from me, and what I could and should do now for others as well as for myself.
dialogical_structure_with_life.citation: Längle, A. (2003). The Art of Involving the Person. European Psychotherapy, 4(1), p. 34.

coping_reactions.reaction: Provisional attitude towards life, planless day-to-day attitude, collective thinking
coping_reactions.source_quote: If man fails systematically to reach meaning, his coping reactions will be a provisional attitude towards life as basic reaction, together with a 'planless, day-to-day attitude toward life' and 'collective thinking' (Frankl 1973, XVI)
coping_reactions.citation: Längle, A. (2002). Existential fundamental motivation. In Motivation, Consciousness and Self-Regulation (pp. 27-42), p. 8.

coping_reactions.source_quote: idealisation and fanaticism as main forms of activism
coping_reactions.citation: Längle, A. (2002). Existential fundamental motivation. In Motivation, Consciousness and Self-Regulation (pp. 27-42), p. 8.
Längle, A. (2002). Existential fundamental motivation. In Motivation, Consciousness and Self-Regulation (pp. 27-42), p. 8.

coping_reactions.reaction: Fatalism, loss of interest, apathy, nihilism
coping_reactions.source_quote: Fatalism (Frankl 1973, XVI), loss of interest, apathy and probably nihilism can be seen as forms of freezing reactions.
coping_reactions.citation: Längle, A. (2002). Existential fundamental motivation. In Motivation, Consciousness and Self-Regulation (pp. 27-42), p. 8.

frankl_1987.description: A possibility against the background of reality
frankl_1987.source_quote: VIKTOR FRANKL (1987, 315) once defined meaning as 'a possibility against the background of reality'.
frankl_1987.citation: Längle, A. (2003). The Art of Involving the Person. European Psychotherapy, 4(1), p. 34.

frankl_1985.description: Valuable possibilities seen in light of meaning and values; fulfilling life task
frankl_1985.source_quote: In another context (Frankl 1985, 57), he referred to the potentialities underlying the meaning: 'The potentialities of life are not indifferent possibilities; they must be seen in the light of meaning and values. At any given time only one of the possible choices of the individual fulfills the necessity of his life task.'
frankl_1985.citation: Längle, A. (2003). The Art of Involving the Person. European Psychotherapy, 4(1), p. 34.

existential_meaning.description: The most valuable, realistic possibility of the given situation, for which one feels one should decide
existential_meaning.source_quote: This notion of valuable possibilities, endorsed by the theory of the fundamental existential motivations, defines meaning even more concretely as the most valuable, realistic possibility of the given situation, for which I feel I should decide myself. Existential meaning is therefore what is possible here and now, on the basis of facts and reality, what is possible for me, may it be what I need now, or what is the most pressing, valuable or interesting alternative now.
existential_meaning.citation: Längle, A. (2003). The Art of Involving the Person. European Psychotherapy, 4(1), pp. 34-35.
existential_meaning.perception_organ: Our sensitivity as well as our moral conscience
existential_meaning.complexity_note: To define and redefine this continually is an extremely complex task

ontological_meaning.description: Overall meaning in which one finds oneself; does not depend on the person
ontological_meaning.source_quote: Apart from this existential meaning we may also consider an ontological meaning. This is the overall meaning in which I find myself and which does not depend on me. It is the philosophical and religious meaning, the meaning the creator of the world must have had in mind. I can perceive it in presentiments and in faith
ontological_meaning.citation: Längle, A. (2003). The Art of Involving the Person. European Psychotherapy, 4(1), p. 35.

chartres_cathedral_story.description: Illustrative story about three stone cutters showing levels of meaning
chartres_cathedral_story.source_quote: It was at the time when the cathedral at Chartres was being built. A traveler came along the way and saw a man sitting at the roadside, cutting a stone. The traveler asked him astonished what he was doing there. 'Don't you see? I am cutting stones!' Nonplussed the traveler continued on his way. Around the next bend, he saw another man, also cutting stones. Again he stopped and asked the same question. 'I am cutting corner-stones,' was the reply. Shaking his head, our man traveled on. After a while he met a third man who was sitting in the dust and cutting stones, just as the others had been. Resolutely he walked up to him and asked: 'Are you also cutting corner-stones?' – The man looked up at him, wiped the sweat from his brow and said: 'I am working at a cathedral.'
chartres_cathedral_story.citation: Längle, A. (2003). The Art of Involving the Person. European Psychotherapy, 4(1), p. 35.

sub_themes.description: Decision about the best possibility in a situation that demands action and personal involvement
sub_themes.source_quote: The existential question of meaning leads up to the decision about the best possibility in a situation, which might also stand as a definition for existential meaning.
sub_themes.citation: Längle, A. (1992). What Are We Looking for When We Search for Meaning? Ultimate Reality and Meaning, 15(4), p. 311.

sub_themes.description: Sequential steps in finding meaning through reality, values, and relations
sub_themes.source_quote: The seeker of meaning first looks for reality, searches for facts and conditions. Perception is followed by an order of valuations. The seeker of meaning involves himself as a sensor of values on the basis of his own self-esteem. At the third step, finally, he transcends himself and enters a personal relation by making a decision.
sub_themes.citation: Längle, A. (1992). What Are We Looking for When We Search for Meaning? Ultimate Reality and Meaning, 15(4), p. 313.

sub_themes.description: What life wants from me and what the moment expects from me
sub_themes.source_quote: The meaningful thing is not only what I can expect from life, but, in accordance with the dialogical structure of existence, it is equally important what life wants from me. And what the moment expects from me, and what I could and should do now for others as well as for myself.
sub_themes.citation: Längle, A. (2003). The Art of Involving the Person. European Psychotherapy, 4(1), p. 34.
indicators: Responding to demands of the hour
What could and should be done for others and self

existential_needs.description: Need to realize possibilities and engage in action that integrates truth, value, and right relations
existential_needs.source_quote: the seeker of meaning is concerned with being, values and justification by ways of relating, which is especially important for psychotherapy.
existential_needs.citation: Längle, A. (1992). What Are We Looking for When We Search for Meaning? Ultimate Reality and Meaning, 15(4), p. 313.

four_fundamental_realities.description: Four cornerstones of existence according to modern existential analytical theory
four_fundamental_realities.source_quote: All preconditions of existence can be summarized in four fundamental structures, the 'cornerstones of existence': • the world in its factuality and potentiality • life with its network of relationships and its feelings • being oneself as a unique, autonomous person • the wider context in which to place oneself = development through one's activities, opening one's future
four_fundamental_realities.citation: Längle, A. (2003). The Art of Involving the Person. European Psychotherapy, 4(1), p. 31.

continuous_confrontation.description: Existence requires continuous confrontation and dialogical exchange with these dimensions
continuous_confrontation.source_quote: Existence in our understanding requires a continuous confrontation and a dialogical exchange with each of these four dimensions. It is on this basis that the subject forms his or her specific notions about reality.
continuous_confrontation.citation: Längle, A. (2003). The Art of Involving the Person. European Psychotherapy, 4(1), p. 31.

dual_nature.description: These realities are both challenging and structures to entrust oneself to
dual_nature.source_quote: These four realities challenge the person to respond, they ask for his or her inner consent, activate his or her inner freedom. But they are not only challenging dimensions – they are also structures which, at the same time, allow one to entrust oneself to each of these given realities.
dual_nature.citation: Längle, A. (2003). The Art of Involving the Person. European Psychotherapy, 4(1), p. 31.

realities.reality: World in its factuality and potentiality
Life with its network of relationships and feelings
Being oneself as unique, autonomous person
Wider context = development through activities, opening future

loss_of_meaning_categories.description: Loss of meaning during illness, suffering, death, or sorrow
loss_of_meaning_categories.source_quote: We observe that the question explicitly forces itself upon man during phases when meaning is lost (Frankl, 1982a, pp. 18ff.; Längle, 1985, p. 85). Here primarily losses of value should be mentioned: During illness, suffering, death or sorrow, which call for a special attitude in man.
loss_of_meaning_categories.citation: Längle, A. (1992). What Are We Looking for When We Search for Meaning? Ultimate Reality and Meaning, 15(4), p. 308.

loss_of_meaning_categories.description: Lack of orientation in work, having everything to live from but nothing to live for
loss_of_meaning_categories.source_quote: Loss of meaning, however, is also a frequent phenomenon in the area of work. Not even success serves as protection. Just at the point where work loses its quality of necessity for life, a vacuum of orientation is formed and causes the afflicted person to indeed have everything he can live from, but nothing more he can live for (Frankl, 1982b, p. 11; pp. 239ff.).
loss_of_meaning_categories.citation: Längle, A. (1992). What Are We Looking for When We Search for Meaning? Ultimate Reality and Meaning, 15(4), p. 308.

loss_of_meaning_categories.description: Living without relating, leading to emptiness and lack of meaning
loss_of_meaning_categories.source_quote: Besides loss of value and lack of orientation in work, lack of relations is another phenomenon causing the existential vacuum (Frankl, 1982a, pp. 7, 18f.). This abounds wherever life is experienced. Living without relating dwindles to boring and joyless consumption.
loss_of_meaning_categories.citation: Längle, A. (1992). What Are We Looking for When We Search for Meaning? Ultimate Reality and Meaning, 15(4), p. 308.

meaning_characteristics.description: Meaning is based on situational reference
meaning_characteristics.source_quote: Accordingly, the psychological understanding of meaning always has four aspects: Firstly it is objective 'on the basis of its situational reference' (Frankl, 1982a, p. 56).
meaning_characteristics.citation: Längle, A. (1992). What Are We Looking for When We Search for Meaning? Ultimate Reality and Meaning, 15(4), p. 308.

meaning_characteristics.description: Meaning is relative to the person and situation linkages
meaning_characteristics.source_quote: Secondly, meaning is relative, with regard to the person it is relating to, as well as to further linkages of the situation itself.
meaning_characteristics.citation: Längle, A. (1992). What Are We Looking for When We Search for Meaning? Ultimate Reality and Meaning, 15(4), p. 308.

meaning_characteristics.description: Meaning can only be recognized and realized by the person involved
meaning_characteristics.source_quote: Thirdly, it is subjective, in that it can only be recognised and realised by the person involved in the respective situation.
meaning_characteristics.citation: Längle, A. (1992). What Are We Looking for When We Search for Meaning? Ultimate Reality and Meaning, 15(4), p. 308.

meaning_characteristics.description: Meaning has a challenging character that urges action
meaning_characteristics.source_quote: meaning is, fourthly, always appellative by its character of challenge (Frankl, 1982a, pp. 52-57), urging the subject with its typical call to 'do something with me!'
meaning_characteristics.citation: Längle, A. (1992). What Are We Looking for When We Search for Meaning? Ultimate Reality and Meaning, 15(4), p. 308.

notes: Version 1.2 adds crucial detail about the motivational process and dialogical structure of existence.
Major additions: Three-step motivational process (recognizing, harmonizing, inner consent); Four-element structure of will; Interpersonal paradigm; Assessment questions for each FM.
The codebook now includes clear operational questions for assessing each FM in participant testimony.
The shift from Frankl's individualistic 'will to meaning' to modern EA's interpersonal/dialogical paradigm is documented.
The concept of 'provocation' as starting point for motivation provides a key indicator for coding participant responses.
Future versions will continue to add depth as more sources are incorporated, particularly focusing on clinical applications and specific indicators.
